newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish employers fret over troubled Bell Lines.
newsitem.headline: Irish employers fret over troubled Bell Lines.

text.p: The Irish employers' group IBEC expressed "serious concern" on Wednesday over reports that plans to rescue the troubled Waterford-based Bell Lines group faced collapse.
"The elimination of this substantial shipping capacity has serious implications for exporters at a time when trade is extremely buoyant," IBEC said in a statement.
"The IBEC Transport council expresses the hope that further action can be taken to ensure that this shipping link is maintained or alternative service provided to the south-east corridor," it said.

"A switch of some or a lot of this traffic to ports where there is already considerable access congestion would exacerbate problems and disrupt logistics systems for major manufacturing companies," it said.
IBEC said that while alternative services could be found at other ports, the expansion of or maintenance of Waterford is a critical part of Ireland's overall shipping strategy.
The loss of business to the Irish Road Haulage sector would also be a matter of serious concern, especially in light of recent haulage disputes in Dublin, it said.
It was commenting on media reports that plans to rescue Bell Lines were on a knife edge because the latest consortium to try to rescue it had pulled out.
According to the reports, the consortium grouped the privately-owned haulage and shipping services company IMARI, ACT Venture Capital and the IAWS Co-Operative Society.
The reports said that examiner David Hughes could decline to extend the period of the examinership unless he finds new investors to shore up the troubled company.
Hughes is due to report to the High Court on Friday.

A previous consortium including Irish Continental Group, NatWest Venture Capital and Citycorp Venture Capital, which together owned 85 percent of Bell Lines, pulled out of a proposed three million pound rescue package at the beginning of June due to opposition from some creditors.
Opposition came mainly from Waterford Harbour Commissioners and the Ministry for Marine which would have acted as guarantor of the port's debts.
Bell Lines, which has trading debts of around 20 million pounds, ran into difficulties in 1995 and 1996 mainly due to a freight price war on the North Sea and competition from the Channel Tunnel.
It employs around 6OO people in Ireland and Europe.
